questions.question: Describe how to set up the water-filled equal-syringe investigation so that no air is trapped, and state what you observe when one plunger is pushed in.
questions.expected_answer: Place both syringes and the tube under the surface of a basin of water, draw water into one syringe, push the other plunger fully in, connect the tube under the surface, then tilt and tap the system to move any bubbles to a nozzle and expel them before drying the outside. When one plunger is pushed in, the other moves out at the same instant and by the same distance, and a load pressing on the second plunger is felt as an equal force on the first; the mechanical advantage is 1.

questions.question: Compare the results for air and for water in the syringe tests, and explain the difference using the idea of compressibility.
questions.expected_answer: With air the second plunger lags, moves less at first and the system feels spongy under load, because a gas can be compressed and part of the push goes into squeezing the air before the pressure is passed on. With water the second plunger moves immediately and fully and the system feels firm, because a liquid cannot be compressed, so all of the push is transferred at once as pressure through the fluid.

questions.question: State what happens to distance and force when a small water-filled syringe drives a larger one of twice the area, and give two conclusions for the design of the rescue device.
questions.expected_answer: The large plunger moves about half the distance but exerts about twice the force, a mechanical advantage of about 2 set by the ratio of the areas; reversed, the small plunger moves twice as far with half the force. Conclusions: use water, filled and connected under the surface to exclude bubbles, with short tubing so the jaws respond at once and hold under load; and choose the syringe sizes to suit the aim, a small syringe driving a large one for a strong grip or the reverse for a wide, fast opening.
